actions.name: Review home/clinic vitals from check-in
actions.result: Temp 98.2°F, HR 88 bpm, RR 18, BP 112/68 mmHg, SpO2 98% on room air (home pulse oximeter reading relayed by father at start of call).

actions.name: Peak expiratory flow via patient's home peak flow meter (coach through 3 attempts, best effort)
actions.result: Best of 3 attempts: 310 L/min. Patient's documented personal best is 420 L/min (73% of personal best).

actions.name: Observe inhaler technique with fluticasone MDI via camera
actions.result: Patient exhales, then presses canister and inhales in one quick sharp breath without a spacer; no breath-hold at end; coordination is poor and much of the dose likely deposits in mouth/throat.

actions.name: Observe albuterol rescue inhaler technique via camera
actions.result: Similar technique issues: no shake visible, quick inhalation, no breath-hold.

actions.name: General appearance / work of breathing via camera
actions.result: Alert, conversational, speaks in full sentences, no accessory muscle use, no audible wheeze at rest, sitting comfortably.

actions.name: Review emergency department visit note from 2 weeks ago
actions.result: ED visit for acute asthma exacerbation triggered by exertion/possible viral URI; treated with nebulized albuterol x3, oral prednisone 40 mg daily x5 days (completed), discharged with instructions to follow up with pediatrics within 1-2 weeks and continue controller inhaler.

actions.name: Review current medication list and refill/pharmacy fill history
actions.result: Fluticasone propionate HFA 110 mcg, 2 puffs BID prescribed 3 months ago (120-dose canister = ~30-day supply at prescribed dosing of 4 puffs/day); pharmacy refill history shows only 1 refill in 3 months (2 canisters total, 240 doses over ~90 days), consistent with roughly 2.5-3 puffs/day average use rather than prescribed 4 puffs/day - partial underuse, less severe than patient's 'when I remember' framing might suggest but still below prescribed dosing.

actions.name: Review growth chart (height, weight, BMI percentile over time)
actions.result: Height 5'9" (175 cm), Weight 152 lb (69 kg), BMI 22.5 kg/m2, 65th percentile for age - tracking stable along growth curve over past 2 years, no concerning change.

actions.name: Review immunization record
actions.result: Up to date for age including annual influenza vaccine this season; no COVID-19 vaccine on file (patient/family declined).

actions.name: Review spirometry from pulmonology referral last year
actions.result: FEV1 82% predicted, FEV1/FVC ratio 0.76 (mildly reduced), with 14% improvement in FEV1 post-bronchodilator - consistent with mild-moderate persistent asthma with reversible airflow obstruction.

actions.name: Allergy/environmental symptom screening tool (structured questionnaire administered via telehealth)
actions.result: Score suggests mild allergic rhinitis symptom burden; tool does not itself specify home exposures — correlate with history obtained directly from patient/caregiver.

actions.name: Visual inspection of nasal mucosa and oropharynx via camera (caregiver-assisted with flashlight)
actions.result: Nasal mucosa appears mildly erythematous with slight boggy quality; oropharynx clear, no exudate or erythema. Findings are nonspecific and should be correlated with symptom history.

artifacts.title: Emergency Department Visit Summary
artifacts.author: Dr. A. Nguyen, Emergency Medicine
artifacts.body:
CHIEF COMPLAINT: Shortness of breath and wheeze x1 day.

HPI: 15-year-old male with known asthma presented with acute dyspnea, wheezing, and cough that began during basketball practice and worsened overnight. Reports using rescue inhaler multiple times with minimal relief prior to arrival. No fever. Family reports possible mild upper respiratory symptoms (congestion) in the preceding days.

EXAM: Moderate respiratory distress on arrival, RR 28, SpO2 93% on room air, diffuse expiratory wheeze bilaterally, mild subcostal retractions.

TREATMENT: Nebulized albuterol x3 with ipratropium first dose, supplemental O2 2L briefly, oral dexamethasone in ED then prescribed prednisone 40 mg daily x5 days to complete at home. Improved to SpO2 98% RA, RR 18, resolved retractions prior to discharge.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS: Continue controller inhaler (fluticasone 110 mcg 2 puffs BID) daily as prescribed, use spacer if available, follow up with primary pediatrician/asthma care within 1-2 weeks, return to ED or call 911 for worsening breathing, blue lips, or inability to speak in full sentences.

Diagnosis: Acute asthma exacerbation, moderate severity.

cells: 2 months ago (1 refill in past 3 months)
Every 4-6 hours as needed for wheeze/cough
Once daily x5 days - course completed

objectives.text: Elicit a structured asthma control history (daytime/nighttime symptoms, rescue inhaler frequency, activity limitation) and recognize poorly controlled persistent asthma despite recent ED treatment.
Identify adherence barriers to the inhaled corticosteroid (forgetting doses, no spacer, embarrassment in front of peers) and connect them to objective evidence of underuse in the record.
Establish confidential adolescent time, explain confidentiality limits, and screen for substance use, successfully eliciting a sensitive disclosure of daily nicotine vaping.
Elicit the new household cat exposure and correlating allergy symptoms through history-taking, and counsel on this modifiable environmental trigger contributing to worsened asthma control.

Correctly interpret home peak flow and spirometry/ACT data in the context of personal best and reference ranges to classify asthma control level and plan next steps within pediatric scope (step up controller therapy per protocol, correct technique, address triggers, offer cessation counseling/referral, no need for ED/pulmonology escalation today given stable vitals).

Recognize and explore a mismatch between the patient's stated controller adherence and objective pharmacy refill/technique evidence, using it as a nonjudgmental teaching moment rather than confrontation.

mismatches.patientClaim: Jaylen says he takes his fluticasone inhaler 'when I remember,' implying inconsistent but regular-ish use.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Medication list/refill history shows only 1 refill in 3 months for a 120-dose canister that should last ~30 days at the prescribed 4 puffs/day (2 canisters = 240 doses over ~90 days, ~2.5-3 puffs/day average) - below the prescribed 4 puffs/day but higher than a casual 'when I remember' framing might suggest, indicating partial but meaningful underuse rather than near-total nonadherence.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Self-reported adherence often doesn't match objective refill data in either direction; refill/pharmacy data and demonstrated technique provide more objective evidence and should be explored supportively, not punitively.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Poorly controlled persistent asthma (ACT score 14/25; peak flow 73% of personal best) in the setting of inhaled corticosteroid underuse/poor technique, a new environmental trigger (household cat), and newly disclosed daily nicotine vaping, following a recent ED visit for exacerbation.
differential: Suboptimal asthma control due to ICS nonadherence and poor inhaler technique (most likely primary driver)
Asthma exacerbation triggered/worsened by new cat exposure (allergic component)
Vaping-associated airway irritation contributing to cough and bronchospasm
Allergic rhinitis with postnasal drip contributing to nighttime cough
Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction superimposed on underlying persistent asthma
keyFindings: Rescue inhaler use 5-6x/week and nocturnal cough 2x/week indicate poorly controlled asthma
Peak flow 310 L/min = 73% of personal best (yellow zone)

Pharmacy refill pattern (1 refill in 3 months, ~2.5-3 puffs/day average) shows ICS use below the prescribed BID dosing despite patient reporting fairly regular partial use, highlighting a gap between self-report and objective data
Poor MDI technique without spacer on camera observation, likely reducing effective lung deposition
New household cat (~6 weeks), elicited on history, with correlating nasal congestion/sneezing
Daily nicotine vaping disclosed for ~4 months, previously undocumented and a plausible contributor to airway irritability
Prior spirometry showing reversible obstruction consistent with persistent asthma, supporting ongoing controller need
Stable current vitals and comfortable work of breathing today, no signs of acute distress requiring emergency referral at this visit
plan: Reinforce and reassess inhaled corticosteroid technique; prescribe/arrange a spacer and demonstrate correct use via video coaching
Address adherence barriers collaboratively: align dosing with existing routines (e.g., tie to toothbrushing), consider discussing simplified regimen with supervising attending if needed

Discuss step-up or confirm appropriate controller therapy with supervising attending/asthma specialist given ongoing poor control despite reported use; consider referral back to pulmonology for reassessment
Elicit and counsel on environmental trigger reduction related to the new cat (e.g., keeping cat out of bedroom, hand-washing, HEPA filtration) while respecting the family's wish to keep the pet

Provide confidential, nonjudgmental brief intervention and counseling on nicotine vaping cessation; offer referral to adolescent-focused tobacco/vaping cessation resources or counseling as appropriate within pediatric scope
Review and update the written asthma action plan with the patient and ensure he can state red-flag symptoms requiring urgent care/ED return

Schedule close follow-up (e.g., 2-4 weeks) to reassess control, technique, and adherence; coordinate with father on general asthma management while maintaining confidentiality about vaping per adolescent consent/confidentiality norms

No indication today for emergency referral given stable vitals, comfortable breathing, and no signs of acute distress; escalate immediately if red-flag symptoms (inability to speak in full sentences, retractions, SpO2 drop) develop
redFlags: Peak flow in red zone (<50% personal best) or inability to speak in full sentences would warrant immediate ED referral
Accessory muscle use, cyanosis, or SpO2 <92% on exam would require urgent escalation
Disclosure of suicidal ideation or severe depression would require immediate safety assessment and escalation beyond routine asthma follow-up
Signs of nicotine withdrawal or escalating substance use pattern warranting more intensive adolescent substance use intervention/referral
educationPoints: Objective measures (ACT score, peak flow versus personal best, pharmacy refill data) often reveal a different picture of control than patient self-report alone and should be used together, not as a 'gotcha'
Confidential adolescent interviewing, explained clearly up front, increases disclosure of sensitive behaviors like vaping that caregivers and prior acute-care encounters may miss entirely
Correct inhaler technique and spacer use substantially affect inhaled corticosteroid efficacy; technique should be observed, not assumed, at every visit
New household pets are a common and modifiable asthma trigger in adolescents and warrant specific screening after any exacerbation, elicited through history rather than assumed
Nicotine vaping is increasingly common among adolescent athletes and can worsen airway reactivity; routine, nonjudgmental screening is part of comprehensive asthma care
Pediatric residents should recognize the limits of their scope and involve supervising attendings or asthma specialists for medication step-up decisions and complex cessation counseling referrals

profile.title: Poorly controlled persistent asthma in a 15-year-old athlete following emergency department visit
profile.summary: A 15-year-old Black male basketball player presents for asthma follow-up two weeks after an ED visit. He has frequent rescue inhaler use and nocturnal symptoms despite prescribed inhaled corticosteroid, which he takes inconsistently and without a spacer. Once confidentiality is established, he discloses daily nicotine vaping for four months and embarrassment about using inhalers in front of teammates. A new household cat and poor adherence contribute to suboptimal control (peak flow 73% of personal best). The case teaches adolescent confidential interviewing, asthma control assessment, identifying adherence barriers and environmental triggers, and shared decision-making around controller therapy intensification and vaping cessation.
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit; patient's bedroom at home in Atlanta
